detail:
NIDDK describes chronic kidney disease (CKD) as a condition in which the kidneys are damaged or have a structural problem that prevents them from filtering blood the way they should, so waste and extra fluid can build up in the body. The institute notes that CKD often develops slowly, that advanced long-lasting CKD typically cannot be reversed, and that in some people it can lead to kidney failure. Diabetes and high blood pressure are described as the most common causes in adults, with heart disease and a family history of kidney disease among the risk factors.

NIDDK notes that many people have no symptoms in the early stages, and that symptoms in later stages can include fatigue, swelling, changes in urination, nausea, and shortness of breath. Because early disease can be silent, sources describe diagnosis as resting on blood and urine testing, including an estimated glomerular filtration rate from a blood test and a urine test for albumin, a protein that can pass into urine when kidney filters are damaged.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about chronic kidney disease testing and symptoms.
sourceName: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
summary: NIDDK explains chronic kidney disease as kidney damage that reduces blood filtering, most commonly caused in adults by diabetes and high blood pressure, often with no early symptoms and diagnosis built on blood and urine tests.
takeaways: damaged kidneys filter blood less well, so waste and fluid can build up
diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes in adults
early CKD often has no symptoms, so blood and urine tests are central to diagnosis
title: Chronic Kidney Disease: when damaged kidneys filter blood less well
